shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Twice as rich. {p} In 1995, the average Japanese person produced more than twice as much as the average Italian, in plain dollars at market exchange rates. About forty-five thousand dollars a year, against about twenty-one thousand. {pp} In 2022, Italy passed Japan, by about a hundred and thirty dollars. {p} This year, in the IMF's numbers, Italy is about thirty percent ahead.

And Italy isn't alone. Spain passed Japan in 2024. In the IMF's forecast, Portugal passes it in 2029. {p} These are not the economies people usually call fast. Italy's economy has grown about ten percent in twenty-five years. {pp} <soft>So this isn't really a story about Southern Europe. It's a story about what happened to Japan's money.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this channel is a series about who's passing whom. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, four lines.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Japan against Italy, Spain and Portugal, in plain dollars per person. {p} In 1995, Japan was more than twice as rich as Italy, almost three times as rich as Spain, and almost four times as rich as Portugal. {pp} Japan peaked in 2012. Then its line goes down, while the other three keep climbing. Italy crosses in 2022. Spain in 2024. And Portugal, in the forecast, in 2029.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded) and GDP per capita in current US$ (NGDPDPC), 2012–2024
shots.title: 2012 to 2024
shots.narration: Here's the strangest part. From 2012 to 2024, after inflation, Japan's economy grew about nine percent. Italy's grew about nine percent too. Almost exactly the same. {pp} But in dollars per person, Japan's number fell by almost a third. Italy's rose by about sixteen percent. {p} Same growth. Opposite dollars. The difference is mostly the currency: the yen lost almost half its value against the dollar. The euro lost much less.

stats.at: Japan's economy grew about nine percent
stats.label: Japan, real growth 2012–2024

stats.at: Italy's grew about nine percent too
stats.label: Italy, real growth 2012–2024

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Now adjust for what money actually buys at home, and the picture changes again. {p} On this measure, Italy was already ahead of Japan in 1990. Japan pulled slightly ahead for a few years, from 2014 to 2017. {pp} Since 2018, Italy has been ahead every year, and this year by about eleven percent. {p} So the old idea of Japan as far richer than Italy was mostly an exchange-rate story.
And if you're enjoying this, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, to be fair to Japan.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · unemployment rate (% of labor force), 2026 estimate
shots.title: Unemployment, 2026
shots.narration: Unemployment this year: about two point five percent in Japan, {pp} five point six in Italy. And when prices jumped in 2022, inflation was about two and a half percent in Japan, and almost nine in Italy. {p} Both carry heavy government debt: about two hundred percent of the economy in Japan, about a hundred and thirty-eight in Italy.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: So who's next? {p} This year, the average Portuguese person produces about ninety-eight percent of what the average Japanese person does, in plain dollars. In the IMF's forecast, Portugal passes Japan in 2029. {pp} And right behind it, Poland: eighty-eight percent this year, and ninety-nine percent in 2031. That one has its own episode on the channel. {p} In 1995, all of these countries together looked poor next to Japan.

<soft>So, what's your guess?</soft> {pp} Does the yen bounce back and put Japan ahead again, {p} or is this the new normal? {pp} Tell me in the comments. {pp} If you're watching from Japan or Italy: {p} does this match what you see? {pp} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, {p} this is the episode where Poland passed Japan, adjusted for prices. {pp} It's right here. {pp} I'm Chartbound. {p} See you in the next one.

checks.say: ITA passed JPN in 2022 by ≈130; ahead every year 2022–2031; 2021 still behind
2012→2024 real: JPN +9%, ITA +9%; USD: JPN −32% (almost a third), ITA +16%
PPP: ITA > JPN in 1990; JPN ahead exactly 2014–2017 (1990–2031); ITA ahead 2018–2031; 2026 ITA +11%
unemployment 2026 JPN 2.5, ITA 5.6; CPI 2022 JPN 2.5, ITA 8.7 (almost nine); debt 2026 JPN ≈ 199 (about two hundred), ITA ≈ 138
1995: JPN > ITA, ESP, PRT, POL (all looked poor next to Japan)

yt.title: Japan Was Twice as Rich as Italy. Now Italy Is 30% Ahead.
yt.description:
Income per person in plain US dollars, at market exchange rates (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 1995 the average Japanese person produced 2.2× as much as the average Italian. Italy passed Japan in 2022; this year it's ~30% ahead. Spain passed Japan in 2024, and in the IMF's forecast Portugal passes it in 2029. The strangest part: from 2012 to 2024 both economies grew ~9% after inflation, yet Japan's dollar income per person fell ~32% and Italy's rose ~16% — the yen. Adjusted for prices, Italy was already ahead in 1990. Plus where Japan still wins (unemployment, inflation) and who's next (Portugal, Poland).

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (NGDPDPC, PPPPC, NGDP_RPCH, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
